title: I used Claude Code to build a light and darkness system for my dark fantasy RPG. Getting it to feel right was the hard part.
author: zanemoore575
selftext:
I've been building Nightfall, a slow, story-driven dark fantasy RPG in Godot. I use Claude Code for much of the implementation, while I handle the game direction, mechanics and design.

One of the systems I've spent a lot of time working on is the lantern.

The basic idea is that the dead are drawn to light, but light also burns them. When your lantern is lit, enemies fighting in its light are weaker, but sleeping enemies can detect you from much further away. In darkness, most of them leave you alone, but anything that does wake up hits considerably harder.

On paper, it's a fairly straightforward mechanic to describe and implement.

I've found Claude can often get a system about 90% of the way there. The remaining 10% is where things get interesting.

I've spent quite a bit of time taking the lantern into actual gameplay, testing encounters, adjusting behaviours and going back and forth with Claude to get things feeling right. It's not enough for the individual mechanics to work. They need to create interesting decisions for the player.

For example, putting your lantern out is almost instant, whereas lighting it leaves you exposed for a few seconds. That creates some interesting situations when you're trying to escape a group of enemies.

It's been a good example of something I've learnt building a game with AI: getting code implemented is one thing, but making the resulting gameplay enjoyable takes a lot of direction, testing and iteration.

Nightfall 0.3.1 has just released on [itch.io](http://itch.io), with various QoL improvements and quest updates. The larger map and third raid are still in development.

[https://middafrostey.itch.io/nightfall](https://middafrostey.itch.io/nightfall)

I'm curious how other people using AI for game development approach that last 10%. Do you find getting something working is relatively straightforward, but getting it to actually feel good is where most of your time goes?
